translation:
One of the principal disciples of Kabirji was Padmanabh, who lived in Patan, Gujarat. He was born into the Prajapati caste, but being influenced by Kabirji's teachings, he went to Kashi (Varanasi) and took initiation (diksha) from him. On his Guru's instruction, Padmanabh returned to Patan and settled there. Padmanabh was born in Patan on Thursday, Chaitra Sud 5, Vikram Samvat 1458.

His father's name was Karan, and his mother's name was Lakshmana; they were householders (grihasthi). His wife's name was Patal Devi. Padmanabh was a very influential person. Seeing his stature, Dhanraj Pandya, the minister (pradhan) of the Patan kingdom at that time, was impressed by him and became his disciple. Later, the Guru and disciple together spread the Ramkabir tradition in Patan and kindled the Kabir school of thought. Because of this, the Suba (governor) Saravarkhar gifted Padmanabh 10 vighas of land, and on that land Padmanabh, together with Dhanraj, established a vadi (garden compound) on Sunday, Kartak Sud 14, Samvat 1470. In Padmanabh's lineage, one high-caliber disciple followed another, and they spread the Kabir school of thought and the Ramkabir tradition widely across Saurashtra and North Gujarat. Padmanabhji does not belong to our own Guru lineage, but Gyaniji Maharaj and Padmanabhji were guru-brothers (disciples under the same guru-line), and both worked together with great cooperation to spread Kabirji's teachings in Gujarat. Jivanji Maharaj was influenced by Padmanabh. He recognized that Dhanraj Pandya's compositions were of high caliber, and had these verses (pado) used in our daily, social, and spiritual customs and rites.

At the Patan vadi, Kabirji's shrine (sthan) has been placed on the basis of the Guru lineage; and since we are followers of the very same Ramkabir tradition, Jivanji Maharaj's kyaro (memorial shrine) has been placed alongside Kabirji's kyaro. The well-known Gujarati writer Dr. Kabhikumar Bhadra wrote a very fine article titled "Kabir Shishya Padmanabhji" ("Padmanabhji, Disciple of Kabir") in the ninth issue of Jivanvani, Year 2, Magshar Sud, 2034. It is well worth reading for inquisitive devotees.
